title: Neuromuscular performance, physiological recovery, and maturation-referenced reference values in youth athletes: A cross-sectional study
content:
by Souhail Bchini, Dhouha Moussaoui, Anissa Bouassida, Nouf H. Alkhamees, Nadhir Hammami, Fatma Hilal Yagin

This cross-sectional study characterized neuromuscular performance and acute physiological responses across age, sex, and biological maturation in 140 youth athletes (74 boys, 66 girls; 10–16 years), and described maturation-stratified distributions of two field measures. Participants completed 30-m sprint, countermovement jump (CMJ), standing long jump (SLJ), and handgrip testing; post-sprint heart-rate recovery (HRrec-30s) and a testing-battery perceived-exertion index (PEI) served as co-primary physiological/perceptual outcomes; maturity offset (Mirwald method) classified Pre-, Circa-, and Post-PHV subgroups; allometric scaling was used to account for body size; and a Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied across a pre-specified family of 58 pairwise comparisons and correlations (Tables 2–6). Boys outperformed girls across all neuromuscular tests (d = 0.63–0.76), whereas HRrec-30s and the perceived-exertion index did not differ significantly by sex. HRrec-30s was more strongly associated with maturity offset than with chronological age (r = 0.52 vs 0.46; η²p for maturation vs age groups 0.43 vs 0.39). Mean HRrec-30s was 27.8 ± 6.2 bpm in the Pre-PHV group and 45.3 ± 8.8 bpm in the Post-PHV group (p < 0.001, FDR-corrected). The perceived-exertion index was lower in more mature groups (7.5 ± 1.2 vs 6.3 ± 1.1). Sex and maturation differences in jump and strength performance remained after allometric scaling, although they were smaller. Maturation-stratified distributions reported here are preliminary and descriptive and are not decision thresholds; prospective, criterion-validated research is needed before they can be recommended for individual athlete monitoring or training-load decision-making.
